content:
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson announced on Tuesday, choosing the day the country celebrates as Victory Day for a comeback that the government in Dhaka says will end in her arrest.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, November 24, Hasina urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her return from Delhi to Dhaka on Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the national carrier. "Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in the statement, [as reported by Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/sheikh-hasina-plans-to-return-to-bangladesh-from-exile-on-december-16).

The date is one of the most charged in Bangladesh's national calendar. December 16 marks the anniversary of the surrender of Pakistani forces in 1971 and the country's emergence as an independent nation after its liberation war. Hasina's choice is deliberately symbolic: her father, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the independence movement, and her Awami League party was the political force behind the liberation struggle. "It is deeply symbolic that she has chosen 16 December, our Victory Day, for her planned return to Bangladesh," Ali said. "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people, honouring the great victory achieved under the leadership of her father."

Tuesday's announcement is the first time Hasina has named a specific date for her return. In August she said she intended to come back by December, but until now she had given no precise day. In a letter emailed to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, Hasina, through her counsel, also asked the acting high commissioner to take the necessary steps to issue new travel and identity documents, after her passport was cancelled in the months following her flight.

The government in Dhaka has rejected the request outright. Hasina can return only through the extradition process under the India-Bangladesh treaty, officials said, and she will be arrested the moment she lands. Abu Abdullah M Saleh, press secretary to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told The Associated Press that the government's position on her extradition as a convict had not changed. Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed. She has rejected the verdict and said she is ready to fight the case once she is back in the country.

Hasina fled to India on August 5, 2024, after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule. Since then, Bangladesh's political landscape has been transformed: the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, led by Tarique Rahman, returned to power in an election, while Hasina's Awami League has been banned. Her planned return therefore lands in a country now governed by the party that was her principal rival for decades, and by a prime minister whose government has repeatedly warned that she faces arrest and a jail term on arrival.

The announcement also comes amid a fresh wave of political violence in Bangladesh. Just last week, the authorities deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops across the country after ten days of bomb blasts and arson attacks linked to Hasina's planned return, as covered in our report on the [paramilitary deployment](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/bangladesh-deploys-paramilitary-hasina-return-unrest-november-2026). The Awami League had called a nationwide lockdown, and the security deployment underlined how combustible her name remains, even from exile.

India's role is now central to whatever happens next. New Delhi has repeatedly said that Dhaka's extradition request for Hasina remains under consideration, and Bangladeshi officials say there have been no official discussions with India about arranging an aircraft to bring her back. Whether India allows her to board a flight, and whether Dhaka would enforce an arrest warrant at the airport, will decide whether December 16 becomes a homecoming or a standoff played out in the open. The Hindu reported that Hasina's camp has framed the demand as a matter of constitutional responsibility, arguing that a government which, in its words, exiled her contrary to the constitution must now make her return possible.

For now, the two sides are talking past each other: Hasina presents her return as a right and a symbolic homecoming on the most sacred date in the national calendar, while the Rahman government treats her as a convicted fugitive who can come home only in custody. December 16 is three weeks away, and the coming days will show whether either side blinks — or whether the Victory Day anniversary becomes the stage for the most dramatic confrontation in Bangladeshi politics since the uprising that drove her from power. The region has already had a tense autumn, with India and Pakistan sliding toward confrontation after the Kashmir attack, as covered in our report on the [Pahalgam crisis](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-pakistan-escalation-pahalgam-attack-november-2026), and a forced return by a former prime minister facing a death sentence would add another flashpoint to South Asia's crowded calendar.

(Photo: Sheikh Hasina in 2023, an archival portrait, not the November 2026 announcement.)
summary: Ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has announced she plans to return to Bangladesh from exile in India on December 16, Victory Day, and asked Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her flight on the national carrier. Dhaka says she can return only through extradition and will be arrested on arrival — she faces a death sentence imposed in absentia.
title: Sheikh Hasina names December 16 for her return to Bangladesh — and Dhaka says she will be arrested on arrival
